newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gore visits island prison where Mandela suffered.
newsitem.headline: Gore visits island prison where Mandela suffered.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore toured the island prison on Sunday where South African President Nelson Mandela was incarcerated for 18 years and said the prisoners' tales were a source of inspiration for the world.

Hosted by South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, whose father Govan Mbeki was imprisoned in the next cell to Mandela, Gore made the half-hour boat trip from Cape Town to Robben Island and walked the narrow corridor to cell number five, a tiny concrete room barely big enough for a bed.
For the first 14 years of his incarceration, Mandela did not have a bed and slept on the bare floor while guards prowled the corridor night and day.

With Gore's wife Tipper and two of his children crowding into the confined space, the vice president peered through the bars at the bleak concrete exercise area outside the window. He viewed the quarry where Mandela and other prisoners hacked out tons of rock under the hot African sun.

"It's a very moving experience. It's unbelievable that so much cruelty continued for so long," Gore told reporters. "But the triumph of the human spirit is the true story of Robben Island. What they endured is unbelievable, just unbelievable."
"Their inspiration goes beyond South Africa to the United States and the rest of the world. I think you're going to see millions of people visit Robben Island in the future," he said.

Mandela was convicted of treason by South Africa's white supremacist rulers in 1963 and sent to Robben Island where he spent the next 18 years. He was then moved to another prison on the mainland for over eight more years before being released in 1990. Four years later, he was elected president in the country's first non-racial elections.

Gore later paid a courtesy call on Mandela and the two discussed the prison visit. Mandela said he would be happy to see the prison turned into a memorial and museum but he did not want it to become a shrine to him.

"I have got serious reservations about a concentration on a single individual when Robben Island represents generations after generations of freedom fighters who opened this battle as far back as 1659," he said.
Gore is in South Africa at the head of a high-level team holding talks aimed at improving cooperation between the two countries on trade, education, health, the energy and the environment.
His guide on Robben Island was Ahmed Kathrada, who spent 21 years in the prison. He described some of the hardships and humiliations the prisoners had to endure at the hands of their white jailers.

For instance, the punishment for not working hard enough at the quarry was six days without food. He said prisoners were allowed one visit and one letter from the outside world every six months and the letter could be no more than 500 words.
The first letter addressed to Kathrada was withheld from him for 18 years because it contained the news that the British Labour Party had won the general election of 1964.
As a special treat, prisoners were allowed to buy a loaf of bread once a year at Christmas.

Kathrada said the wardens addressed prisoners as "boy" and made them wear shorts. They tried to discriminate between the races, giving the prisoners of Indian or white descent more food than the blacks. Despite the extreme conditions, the prisoners set up what became a virtual university, teaching themselves a variety of academic disciplines.
Plans are underway to build a memorial on the island and Kathrada said he was anxious it should sent the right message to the world.
"While we had hardship and suffering here, we wouldn't like Robben Island remembered just as a place to mark our suffering and hardship," he said.

"That is part of history, that should be portrayed. But the message of Robben Island should be the triumph of the human spirit. The triumph of the forces of good over the forces of evil, of justice over injustice, in other words the triumph of the new South Africa over the old."
